questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.question_text: During an autopsy of an individual found dead in an apartment 48 hours post-mortem during a mild spring season, the forensic pathologist observes a distinct greenish discoloration localized specifically over the right iliac fossa. What chemical process is primarily responsible for generating this initial external sign of putrefaction?

options.A: Bacterial breakdown of melanocytes producing melanin residue
options.B: Interaction of cecal bacterial hydrogen sulfide ($H_2S$) with hemoglobin to form sulfhemoglobin
options.C: Acute systemic pooling of deoxygenated venous blood following cardiac standstill
options.D: Fungal synthesis of copper-dependent porphyrin compounds inside the abdominal wall

questions.explanation: Putrefaction: first sign is greenish discoloration of right iliac fossa (cecal bacteria: H2S + Hb → green sulfhemoglobin). Then marbling, bloating, skin slippage. Rate influenced by temperature and environment.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.question_text: An institutional investigator reviews a medical-legal case where a patient died within an unconditioned room. The core body temperature recorded 1 hour post-mortem unexpectedly demonstrated an absolute rise instead of a gradual fall. In which clinical scenario is this phenomenon of post-mortem caloricity classically expected?

options.A: Suicidal ingestion of a massive dose of oral benzodiazepines
options.B: Fatal poisoning with strychnine or death following status epilepticus
options.C: Accidental hypothermic immersion in an ice-water lake
options.D: Sudden terminal myocardial infarction during quiet sleep

questions.explanation: PM caloricity: rise in body temperature after death. Seen in: strychnine poisoning (convulsions continuing after death), tetanus, status epilepticus, typhoid, pontine hemorrhage.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.question_text: A body is discovered at a crime scene, and the initial physical evaluation demonstrates that rigor mortis is firmly established in the muscles of the jaw and face, but has not yet fully locked the lower skeletal extremities. What rule or law governs this predictable, sequential craniocaudal progression of muscular rigidity?
questions.explanation: Rigor mortis: follows Nysten's law — starts in jaw/neck, then trunk, then lower limbs. Onset: 1-2 hours. Maximum: 12 hours. Passes off: 36-48 hours. Due to ATP depletion → actin-myosin cross-linking.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.question_text: During an autopsy of an unidentified decomposed body pulled from an arid terrain, the pathologist observes that the skin and tissues are hard, dry, brittle, dark brown, and structurally intact, completely arresting the typical liquefactive putrefactive process. What is this unique post-mortem phenomenon?
questions.explanation: Mummification is a modification of putrefaction characterized by the dehydration and drying of the body tissues, which turn brown/black and leathery. It requires a hot, dry, airy environment and preserves the structural configuration of the features and wounds.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.question_text: A 32-year-old soldier is shot through the medulla oblongata during a highly stressful, intense hand-to-hand combat engagement. Immediately upon death, his right hand completely skips the initial phase of post-mortem flaccidity and instantly rigidifies, tightly clamping the handle of his combat knife. What is the diagnosis and the underlying pathophysiological differentiation from standard rigor mortis?

options.A: Early onset rigor mortis; driven by sudden cold ambient temperatures
options.B: Cadaveric spasm (Instantaneous rigor); driven by extreme terminal nervous tension and immediate regional ATP depletion
options.C: Post-mortem lividity fixation; driven by rapid hemolysis
options.D: Heat stiffening; driven by immediate denaturation of muscular structural actin proteins

questions.explanation: Cadaveric spasm (instantaneous rigor) occurs at the exact moment of death without a preceding stage of primary flaccidity. It is typically associated with sudden, violent deaths accompanied by intense emotional tension or physical exhaustion (e.g., battlefields, drowning, suicides), resulting in immediate localized ATP depletion that preserves the last voluntary act.
